hook: Researchers just turned raw silk into a transparent, plastic-like material strong enough to potentially power future 6G networks.

sections.voiceover: Researchers just turned raw silk into a transparent, plastic-like material strong enough to potentially power future 6G networks.
sections.visual_cue: Close-up macro shot of shimmering silk fibers transitioning into a clear, solid sheet.

sections.voiceover: How do researchers from Tufts University and Imperial College London turn silk into 6G hardware?
sections.visual_cue: Graphic showing the University of Michigan logo beside a diagram of compressed silk fibers.
b_roll: Laboratory equipment for high pressure testing
Microscopic view of crystalline silk structures

sections.voiceover: This team forces silk to twist terahertz waves, high-frequency light pulses that carry massive data loads.
sections.visual_cue: Abstract animation showing light waves twisting through a crystalline grid structure.

sections.voiceover: To fuse the fibers, the team heated them between 257 and 419 degrees Fahrenheit. Chemical Engineering reports this process forces water out, fusing silk into a single solid sheet.
sections.visual_cue: Chart showing temperature and pressure ranges rising on a scale.
b_roll: Pressure gauge needle moving through high range

sections.voiceover: Engineers use this preserved crystalline structure to build the essential hardware for future 6G networks.
sections.visual_cue: Wide shot of a modern fiber optic lab setting.
